name: Maine
note: In Maine the funeral director files the death certificate, or the family does as an 'authorized person' when no funeral director is used. It goes to the municipal clerk where the death occurred or to the State Registrar of Vital Statistics in DHHS, through the DAVE electronic death registration system. A physician, nurse practitioner or physician associate certifies the cause, unless the death is a medical examiner case. Nobody may bury or cremate a body without a disposition permit from the clerk or the State Registrar, and cremation also needs a medical examiner's release. The registered death reaches municipal clerks, the voter-roll registrar (who must review death records), the Maine Health Data Organization and national statistics. Certified copies go to a wide list of relatives and to anyone with a 'direct and legitimate interest', and are issued by DHHS or by the municipalities of death and of residence.

steps.title: Report medical examiner cases to the Office of Chief Medical Examiner
steps.who: Whoever must report under 22 M.R.S. § 3026; § 3025 lists the circumstances.
steps.trigger: Death by injury or poisoning, sudden death in apparent good health, death in custody or in a DHHS facility, child deaths not clearly natural, or no attending physician able to certify natural causes.
steps.summary: The Chief Medical Examiner decides whether to accept a reported death as a medical examiner case and may refer natural deaths back to the attending physician to certify. In an accepted case, the medical examiner completes the medical certification and is responsible for identity, time, place, cause and manner of death.

steps.title: Certify the cause of death
steps.who: A physician, nurse practitioner or physician associate who knows the patient's recent medical condition. For a nursing-home resident not seen within 48 hours (two weeks if terminally ill), the provider must first examine the body.
steps.trigger: A death that is not a medical examiner case.

deadline.text: within 24 hours after receipt of the certificate (rule); 48 hours after death if the physician originates it

steps.summary: Certification must be 'timely' as the department's rule specifies, and is done in the DAVE electronic system. The State Registrar must report a provider who fails to certify in time to the provider's licensing board.

steps.title: File the death certificate with the municipal clerk or State Registrar
steps.who: The funeral director, or the 'authorized person' in charge of disposition: immediate family, the domestic partner, or someone they or the deceased authorised in writing.
steps.trigger: The death; before the body is removed from the State.

deadline.text: within three days after the day on which death occurred (ch. 1); ch. 5 says five days

steps.summary: The statute leaves the time limit to department rule. Two rules conflict: the disposition rule says three days and the medical certification rule says five. Funeral directors and certifiers must use the DAVE electronic death registration system. Family members acting as authorized persons file a paper VS-3 form with the state office, which keys it in. Neglecting a registration duty is a strict-liability Class E crime.

steps.title: Obtain a disposition (burial-transit) permit
steps.who: The funeral director or authorized person, from the municipal clerk (or a subregistrar) where death occurred or where the funeral establishment is, or from the State Registrar.
steps.trigger: Intended burial, cremation, natural organic reduction or removal from the State.
steps.summary: No body may be buried, cremated or removed until the permit is obtained. A non-funeral director gets a permit only after a medical certificate is received from a practitioner who personally examined the body. Moving a body without a permit is a crime.

steps.title: Medical examiner's release before cremation or removal
steps.who: A duly appointed medicolegal death investigator or medical examiner.
steps.trigger: Disposition by cremation, burial at sea, medical science, natural organic reduction or removal from the State.
steps.summary: The clerk or State Registrar may issue a permit for these forms of disposition only on receiving the medical examiner's certificate, which serves as a second check on deaths not referred to the medical examiner.

steps.title: Municipal clerk forwards death records to the State Registrar and the residence municipality
steps.who: The clerk of the municipality where the death occurred.

deadline.text: within 7 days after receipt, on a weekly basis

steps.summary: The clerk checks the record and sends it to the State Registrar. At the same time the clerk sends a copy to the municipality where the deceased lived, if that is different. The rule dates from 1996, before DAVE, which now holds records centrally.

steps.title: Certified copies for relatives and people with a direct and legitimate interest
steps.who: The registrant's spouse, registered domestic partner, descendants, parents, grandparents, siblings, step-relatives, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, parents-in-law, personal representative or designated attorney or agent, and anyone with a direct and legitimate interest. Anyone may get a non-certified copy 25 years after the death. Genealogists with researcher cards may get non-certified copies.
steps.summary: Copies are issued by Data, Research and Vital Statistics or by the municipal clerk of the place of death or of residence. A refusal can be reviewed by the Superior Court.

steps.title: Voter registrar reviews death records and cancels registrations
steps.who: The municipal registrar of voters; the Secretary of State also maintains the central voter registration system.
steps.trigger: Death records in the clerk's office or provided by the DHHS Office of Vital Records.
steps.summary: The registrar must review death records held by the clerk or provided by DHHS and update the central voter registration system. A published obituary or a signed notice from an immediate family member may also be used. The old 'list of deceased residents' subsection, § 161(3), was repealed in 2005.

steps.title: Death data to the Maine Health Data Organization
steps.who: The State Registrar, to the Maine Health Data Organization.
steps.summary: The State Registrar reports registration data, including identifying health information, to the MHDO, which links it with its other health data under a joint rule.

steps.title: Copies and data to the national vital statistics agency
steps.who: The State Registrar, to the federal agency that compiles national vital statistics.
steps.summary: The national agency may be furnished the copies or data it needs, with the cost reimbursed. The data may not be used to identify individuals unless the State Registrar authorises it.

steps.title: Death certificate data to hospitals and health care practitioners
steps.who: Licensed hospitals and health care practitioners.
steps.summary: The only statutory private-sector route found. Banks, insurers and other private bodies rely on a certified copy, which is available to anyone with a direct and legitimate interest.

steps.title: Published notice to creditors
steps.who: The personal representative appointed by the probate court.
steps.summary: A notice runs once a week for two weeks in a newspaper in the county of domicile, and claims are barred four months after first publication. Separately, municipal clerks may print the year's deaths (name, age, date and place) in the annual town report.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: The statute leaves the limit to rule. 10-146 CMR ch. 1 says three days after the day of death (and before removal from the State); ch. 5 says five days. The shorter is used.

informantDuty.note: The funeral director, or the family as an 'authorized person' when no funeral director is engaged, is responsible for filing.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No review of every certificate. A medical examiner's release is required before cremation, burial at sea, use by science, natural organic reduction or removal from the State.

electronicRegistration.note: Everyone who completes or files a death certificate (funeral directors, certifiers, medical examiners) must use the DAVE electronic death registration system. Only family 'authorized persons' are exempt; they file a paper VS-3 with the state office.

centralPopulationRegister.note: No population register; the State Registrar is custodian of the vital records file.

governmentPropagation.note: Under state law, a registered death reaches the residence municipality, the Maine Health Data Organization and national statistics without any request. Voter registrars must review DHHS death records. No state provision found reaches the BMV, MaineCare or Maine Revenue Services. Federal feeds (SSA) are in the us-federal layer.

certificateAccess.note: A broad list of relatives plus anyone with a direct and legitimate interest. Open non-certified copies after 25 years; genealogists with researcher cards get non-certified copies.

gaps: No Maine statute on who may pronounce death was found. § 2843 and rule ch. 1 only require that the certifier has personally examined the body before a permit issues to a non-funeral director.

The filing deadline conflicts between 10-146 CMR ch. 1 (three days) and ch. 5 (five days). Both rules date from before DAVE (effective 1978/1987, converted 1996), and no newer DAVE rule under § 2847 was found on the Secretary of State's rules page.
Pointer 21-A § 161 no longer carries the death list: § 161(3), 'List of deceased residents', was repealed by PL 2005, c. 453. The operative provision is 21-A § 128, cited instead.
22 M.R.S. § 3026 (the duty to report medical examiner cases and who must report) was not fetched. The step relies on § 3025 and § 2842(3).
No state statute was found sending deaths to the BMV (driver licence cancellation), MaineCare or Maine Revenue Services. Titles 29-A and 36 were not searched exhaustively.
No Maine provision read here mentions an electronic death feed to SSA. It is left to the us-federal layer.
privateSectorVerification is left to the us-federal layer (LADMF). State law gives only hospitals and health care practitioners a data route (§ 2706(5-A)); banks rely on certified copies.
